title: EVERYBODY MAKES MISTAKES… BUT WHEN DOES A MISTAKE BECOME A CHOICE?
paragraphs: EVERYBODY MAKES MISTAKES… BUT WHEN DOES A MISTAKE BECOME A CHOICE?
Grace will forgive the sinner who falls—but grace was never given to make peace with the sin that keeps pulling us back.
There is a sentence we use when the truth gets too close.
When somebody confronts what we did.
When our conscience starts whispering the thing we desperately do not want to hear.
Every one of us has failed.
Every one of us has said something we wish we could pull back into our mouths.
Every one of us has entertained thoughts we would never want projected onto a screen.
Every one of us has disappointed someone.
Every one of us has looked into the mirror and seen a version of ourselves we promised we would never become.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
The person reading this while quietly carrying something nobody knows.
But here is where one of the most dangerous lies can quietly enter the Christian life.
Because “everybody makes mistakes” can begin as an admission of human weakness…
and slowly become permission to keep choosing what Jesus died to free us from.
There is a difference between falling into sin and making a home there.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you toward Christ and rebellion that uses Christ as an excuse.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus, I fell again. Please help me,” and saying, “Jesus will forgive me anyway, so why stop?”
More than we may want to admit.
Imagine someone standing at the edge of the same hole for the hundredth time.
The second time, perhaps he stumbled.
But eventually he memorized the road.
He knows where the hole is.
He knows the promises he will make at 2:00 in the morning.
He knows the prayer he will pray.
At some point we have to ask the terrifying question:
Am I merely making a mistake…
or have I started protecting the sin I keep asking God to forgive?
Paul anticipated almost exactly this distortion of grace.
After explaining the astonishing abundance of God's grace, he asks in Romans 6:1:
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
“What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
The crucial word is ἐπιμένωμεν — epimenōmen, from epimenō.
It carries the idea of remaining, continuing, persisting.
Paul is not asking whether a Christian will ever stumble again.
He is confronting the idea of continuing in sin because grace is available.
Then Paul asks how those who died to sin can still live in it (Romans 6:2). The Greek text itself makes the contrast unmistakable: grace is not Paul's permission slip for remaining under sin's rule.
Grace is not God's way of saying sin does not matter.
Sin mattered enough that Christ bled.
Grace is God's astonishing answer to sin.
And that means grace does not merely say,
Grace begins teaching the forgiven sinner,
“You don't have to remain who you were.”
Because someone reading this has probably been fighting the same battle for years.
Maybe greed dressed up as ambition.
Maybe jealousy you would never admit publicly.
Maybe you keep returning to someone you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
But God has seen every midnight.
And here is where this message could become cruel if we stopped too soon.
Because conviction without the Gospel would leave us staring at our filth.
But Jesus does not expose darkness merely to humiliate people.
He brings darkness into the light so captives can become free.
Listen carefully to the balance Scripture gives us.
“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.”
“καὶ ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ, παράκλητον ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν δίκαιον.”
“But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” (1 John 2:1)
That single verse destroys two lies at once.
“I write… so that you may not sin.”
“You sinned again. God must be finished with you.”
“If anyone does sin, we have an Advocate.”
The reality is that believers can still fall.
And the hope of the fallen believer is not his flawless performance.
That means your failure does not have to become your identity.
But neither should grace become your alibi.
There is a devastating difference between struggling against sin and surrendering to it.
A struggling believer may fall repeatedly and hate that he keeps falling.
He asks trusted believers to walk with him.
Sometimes his progress feels painfully slow.
But somewhere inside him there is still war.
The person making peace with sin begins doing something different.
He stops fighting and starts defending.
And suddenly grace—the very grace purchased at immeasurable cost—has been turned into camouflage for rebellion.
Please hear this without running into the opposite ditch.
Repeated failure does not automatically prove that your repentance is fake.
Some habits have roots that reach deep into wounds, patterns, environments, relationships, and years of practiced behavior.
Sanctification is real, but Christians do not mature at identical speeds.
The answer to repeated failure is therefore not hopelessness.
Bring the sin into the light.
Stop protecting the doorway through which it keeps entering.
Repair what your sin has damaged where possible.
Run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Because repentance is more than feeling horrible after sin.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Repentance does not mean you will never stumble again.
It means you can no longer comfortably call darkness home.
He did not merely make an embarrassing mistake.
And when pressure came, Peter collapsed.
Imagine the moment the rooster crowed.
Imagine realizing that the warning you thought you were strong enough to overcome had just become reality.
Luke tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
That could have been the final chapter.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ met the disciple who had denied Him.
And grace did not restore Peter so Peter could return comfortably to denying Jesus.
Grace restored Peter so he could follow Jesus.
That is the part we sometimes miss.
Jesus does not rescue us so we can lovingly carry our chains back into the prison.
And maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps the Holy Spirit has already put something in your mind while you have been reading.
You didn't need me to name it.
The habit you keep calling “a mistake” even though you have been planning when you will do it again.
What are you asking Jesus to forgive that you are still arranging your life to repeat?
But perhaps uncomfortable is exactly where healing begins.
There is no Gospel in pretending you never sinned.
There is also no Gospel in deciding sin owns you forever.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He went willingly to the cross.
And forgiveness is not offered because you finally became impressive enough for God.
So stop trying to clean yourself enough to approach Him.
And when you fall, do not run away from the only One who can restore you.
But don't crawl toward Jesus asking Him to forgive the chain while your other hand refuses to let it go.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where the person you became collides with the Savior who already knows what you did.
This is where Satan whispers, “You're finished,” while the Gospel declares that Christ still saves sinners.
And maybe today you need to stop saying, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
I don't want to defend it anymore.
I don't want to hide it anymore.
I don't want to use Your grace as permission to remain unchanged.
Teach me to hate what is destroying me and love what draws me closer to You.
When I fall, bring me back.
When I am tempted, give me strength.
When I begin making excuses, expose them.
You do not have to publish the details of private sin. God does not require public oversharing to prove repentance. But sometimes three honest words can become the moment someone stops pretending.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't weaponize this article against them.
Not because you expect to fail, but because temptation has a way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday.
Come back when “just once more” begins sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you not to pray.
Come back when you need to remember:
Grace is not permission to remain in chains.
And not because somebody who truly loves God must prove that love by paying us.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue, reach more people, develop more resources, and put biblical encouragement in front of people who may never walk voluntarily through a church door.
Give freely, prayerfully, and never from manipulation or guilt. As Paul teaches concerning Christian generosity, giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Jesus Christ is still the message.
His Gospel is still the hope.
So share if it may reach somebody.
Follow if you want to keep walking through Scripture with us.
Because the most dangerous thing about repeated sin is not that you made another mistake.
It is that, little by little, you may stop calling darkness darkness.
And the most beautiful thing about grace is not that Jesus gives you permission to keep returning to the grave.
It is that the risen Christ calls you out of it.
You may have returned to the same sin a hundred times—but today does not have to become one hundred and one.
